content: 1. Wearing or removing the circumcision device can cause discomfort and produce an unpleasant odor. 2. The procedure itself may lead to complications, which should be carefully considered. 3. The time required to perform the procedure is a factor that needs to be taken into account. 4. The necessity of follow-up visits after the procedure can be burdensome for patients and their families. 5. The time it takes for individuals to return to their normal daily activities post-procedure is an important consideration. 6. There is significant uncertainty and variability in how much people value the main outcomes of voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC). 7. It is unclear how young adolescent boys, their parents or guardians, and the community prioritize the main outcomes of VMMC. 8. No direct evidence was found regarding the relative values and preferences of young adolescent boys, their parents, or the community concerning VMMC for boys aged 10–14 years. 9. However, indirect evidence suggests key factors influencing the decision to undergo VMMC at this age range, such as acceptability, are available. 10. The acceptability of VMMC among key stakeholders, including parents and adolescents, varies. 11. Four studies on the acceptability of VMMC were included, all of which used cross-sectional designs and structured interviews. 12. Sample sizes ranged from 359 to 1,526 participants, covering regions in Africa (Rwanda, South Africa, Tanzania, Zimbabwe) and India. 13. Three studies assessed parents’ acceptability of VMMC for their children, while two studies focused on acceptability among young and older adolescent boys. 14. No data were available from healthcare providers, policymakers, or funders. 15. Sampling methods varied, with one study using probability proportional to size sampling and others using convenience sampling. 16. One study used a nationally representative sample, while another ensured representation of various ethnicities and geographic contexts. 17. Findings from smaller studies may not be generalizable to other populations. 18. Young adolescents cited protection from HIV/STIs, improved hygiene, and parental or school advice as motivations for undergoing VMMC. 19. Pain was a common barrier to VMMC uptake among younger adolescents. 20. Older men often cited age as a reason for not wanting circumcision, while younger men, particularly those under 19, expressed fear of pain. 21. Parents identified HIV risk reduction as a key facilitator for VMMC acceptability. 22. After being informed about the 60% reduction in HIV risk with circumcision, 79% of parents supported VMMC for their sons, with 89% preferring it to be done before age 15. 23. Parents who had circumcised their sons cited religion, doctor’s advice, health reasons, and wanting their child to resemble their father as motivations. 24. For parents who had not circumcised their children, motivations to change their minds included HIV prevention, knowledge of healing time, understanding the procedure, and minimal pain. 25. Factors such as performing the procedure in a safe hospital setting, offering it free of charge, and cultural acceptance were also important in determining VMMC acceptability. 26. Prepubertal circumcision in a medical setting was preferred due to faster wound healing, less bleeding and pain, and no loss of productivity during recovery. 27. Cost-effectiveness analyses suggest that focusing VMMC on males aged 15–34 years is the most cost-effective strategy. 28. Circumcising younger boys aged 10–14 years results in higher costs per HIV infection averted compared to older adolescents. 29. However, VMMC is a one-time intervention with lifetime benefits, and focusing only on short-term outcomes may overlook its long-term cost-effectiveness. 30. Most males aged 10–14 years are not yet sexually active, so the benefits of VMMC in preventing HIV may not be immediately apparent. 31. Excluding younger adolescents from VMMC programs could lead to unintended consequences, such as loss to follow-up or negative community perceptions of VMMC. 32. Providers and facility managers emphasized the need for adolescent-specific training and refresher courses to ensure accurate and comprehensive information is provided. 33. Counseling approaches for younger adolescents often exclude detailed discussions of sexual health, as they are perceived to have limited sexual experience. 34. Older adolescents are more likely to receive counseling on sexual topics, as they are considered more likely to have started exploring their sexuality. 35. The lack of adolescent-specific training and limited refresher courses for providers was highlighted as a barrier to effective implementation. 36. Cultural differences among countries or sites were not adequately accounted for in the qualitative study, limiting its generalizability. 37. Overall, VMMC for boys aged 10–14 years may be acceptable if concerns about pain and knowledge of procedural care are addressed, weighed against the benefits of HIV prevention.
